title: Christmas Day (John 1:1–18)
hook: the day Mass reads the Word made flesh

segments.voice: Yesterday, Midnight Mass: an emperor, a manger, shepherds on the night shift. Your line was a light at midnight. Who did you think of, working while others slept? Day six hundred forty.

Come back to church on Christmas morning, and something odd happens. The gospel has no manger. No shepherds, no angels, no star, no donkey, no inn. Mary isn't named. Bethlehem isn't mentioned. Instead the reader starts before the world existed, with three words that echo the first line of Genesis: in the beginning. The night Mass told what happened in a stable. The day Mass tells who was born there. Today's word is the feast's own name.
screen: `NO MANGER, NO SHEPHERDS.` → `IN THE BEGINNING.` → `WHO WAS BORN THERE.`

segments.voice: Nativity comes from the Latin nativitas, a birth. The Church's formal name for December 25 is the Nativity of the Lord. And its daytime gospel is the prologue of John, eighteen verses that read like a poem. In the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Word, in Greek, is logos: speech, reason, the meaning behind things. John says this Word made everything, that in him was life, and the life was the light of people. "And the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it." The old word comprehend can mean understand, or grasp, even overpower; the Greek allows both, and translators have argued about it for centuries. Then the line the whole day turns on: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Flesh, not spirit dressed up as a man. Skin, hunger, a body that could get cold. The word for dwelt literally means pitched a tent, the way God's presence lived in a tent among the Israelites in the desert. Catholics mark this line with their bodies. Each Sunday at the Creed, people bow at the words about the incarnation; on Christmas, and on the Annunciation, they kneel. Luke and John are telling the same Christmas from two ends. Luke says: here is a baby, wrapped and laid in a trough. John says: that baby is the Word that was there in the beginning. Put them together and you have the whole surprise of the day.
screen: `NATIVITAS: A BIRTH.` · `IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD.` · `THE LIGHT SHINETH IN DARKNESS.` · `HE PITCHED HIS TENT AMONG US.` · then, large: `THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit a crib, a nativity scene, in a church, a store window, a neighbor's yard, or on a shelf at home. If you can't go, picture one you remember. Saint Francis of Assisi is said to have set up a living one in a cave at Greccio in 1223, with a real ox and donkey, so people could see how poor the birth was. Sit before your crib, real or remembered. Look at the smallest figure. If you pray, you can say John's line, the Word was made flesh. If you don't, just look. The bell holds the time.
Nativity. From the Latin for birth; the Church's name for Christmas, the Nativity of the Lord, when the Word was made flesh. Today's word.
Your line: the word made flesh. Today, do one bodily kindness: food, warmth, a hand on a shoulder. Day six hundred forty.

howItsDone: At the Mass during the Day on Christmas, Catholics hear the prologue of John's Gospel, and at the Creed the congregation kneels at the words about the incarnation.

myth: the Christmas day gospel has the shepherds
it's John's prologue: no manger, no shepherds, just in the beginning.
Catholics kneel at the Creed on Christmas
at the words about the incarnation, on Christmas and the Annunciation.
dwelt among us, in the Greek, pictures a tent
the Word pitched his tent among us.

fork.setup: you're writing a gospel. you could start Jesus's story at his birth, or his baptism. where does John start?
fork.reveal: in the beginning was the Word. John goes back before the world, then says that Word was made flesh.

original.note: Greek: the Word became flesh, John 1:14.

trapdoor: what you thought: Nativity means the crib scene.
what it means: the birth of the Lord, the feast's own name, when Catholics hear that the Word was made flesh.
what a scholar hears: John's eskēnōsen, pitched his tent, recalls God's dwelling in the desert tabernacle; katelaben in 1:5 can mean grasp or overpower.
